headline: Bank of England expected to raise interest rates to 4% on Thursday as inflation climbs to 3.5%

terms.meaning: The main interest rate set by the Bank of England, which influences what banks charge for loans and pay on savings.
The speed at which prices rise over time.
The group of nine experts at the Bank of England who vote on interest rates.

levels.headline: Bank of England expected to raise interest rates to 4% on Thursday as inflation climbs to 3.5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England is widely expected to raise Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points, from 3.75% to 4%, when its Monetary Policy Committee announces its decision on Thursday 5 November. Money markets put the chance of a rise at about 98%, according to LSEG data cited by CNBC.
The expectation follows UK consumer price inflation rising to 3.5% in the 12 months to September, above the 3.4% economists had forecast. Services inflation has also picked up, which fuels worry about second-round effects beyond energy prices. Energy costs linked to the Iran conflict and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz are the main driver.
In September the committee voted 6 to 3 to hold at 3.75%, with three members preferring a rise to 4%, as in July. Trading Economics says markets see further increases possible in February and July. Five-year fixed mortgage rates reached 5% in September, the highest since October 2023.
levels.why: Bank Rate sets the cost of borrowing across the economy, from mortgages to business loans.

levels.headline: Bank of England set to lift interest rates to 4% this week as inflation rises
levels.body:
The Bank of England is expected to raise Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4% on Thursday 5 November. Financial markets see a rise as almost certain, with a 98% chance priced in, according to LSEG.
The main reason is inflation, the rate at which prices rise. It reached 3.5% in the year to September, higher than the 3.4% forecast. Prices for services such as hospitality and transport have also climbed faster, which suggests higher energy costs are feeding into the wider economy. Those costs are tied to the Iran conflict and disruption near the Strait of Hormuz.
The Bank's rate-setting committee voted 6 to 3 to keep rates unchanged in September, with three members already wanting a rise. Markets think more increases could follow in February and July. Mortgage rates have already risen, with five-year fixed deals reaching 5% in September.
levels.why: A rise would make borrowing dearer for homeowners and businesses, while helping savers a little.

levels.headline: Bank of England likely to raise rates this week as inflation picks up
levels.body:
The Bank of England is expected to raise its main interest rate, Bank Rate, from 3.75% to 4% on Thursday. Traders think this is close to certain.
The Bank wants to bring inflation back down to its 2% target. Inflation is the rise in prices over a year, and it climbed to 3.5% in September, a little more than experts had predicted. Higher energy costs, linked to the conflict involving Iran and problems for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, are the main cause. The price of services is also rising faster, which worries the Bank because it can mean higher costs are spreading.
In September, six of the nine members of the rate-setting committee voted to leave the rate alone, while three wanted a rise. Markets think further increases are possible next year. Five-year fixed mortgage deals have already reached around 5%.
levels.why: Interest rate decisions change what people pay on mortgages and earn on savings.

levels.headline: Interest rates expected to rise to 4% as UK inflation climbs
levels.body:
The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates on Thursday, from 3.75% to 4%. Almost everyone in the financial markets expects this.
The Bank raises rates to slow price rises. UK inflation reached 3.5% in the year to September, higher than forecast and well above the Bank's 2% target. Energy prices are a big reason, because of the Iran conflict and trouble for oil and gas shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Prices for services have also gone up faster.
The Bank's committee voted 6 to 3 to keep rates steady in September, but three members wanted a rise. Some investors think there could be more rises in February and July. Mortgage costs have already gone up. Five-year fixed rates hit 5% in September, the highest since October 2023.
levels.why: Higher rates mean bigger mortgage bills for some families but better returns for savers.

levels.headline: Bank of England expected to put up interest rates this Thursday
levels.body:
The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates this Thursday, 5 November, from 3.75% to 4%. People who trade in financial markets think this is almost certain to happen.
The reason is inflation, which means prices going up. In the year to September, prices rose by 3.5%. That is more than experts expected and above the Bank's target of 2%. Fuel and energy have become more expensive because of the conflict involving Iran and problems for ships using the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route for oil. The cost of services, such as eating out, is also rising faster.
A committee of nine people decides the rate. In September, six voted to keep it the same and three wanted it higher. Many mortgage deals already cost more, with typical five-year fixed deals at about 5%.
levels.why: Interest rates affect what you pay to borrow money and what you earn from saving.

levels.headline: Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates on Thursday
levels.body:
The Bank of England is expected to raise its main interest rate on Thursday 5 November, from 3.75% to 4%. Almost everyone who follows the money markets thinks this will happen.
The Bank does this because prices are rising too fast. Prices went up 3.5% in the year to September, and the Bank wants them to rise by only 2%. Fuel and energy cost more because of the conflict involving Iran and problems for oil ships. Bills for services, such as eating out, are rising faster too.
A higher rate makes borrowing dearer, so people tend to spend less, and that slows price rises. Some mortgage deals already cost more. A five-year fixed deal reached about 5% in September, the highest for nearly two years.
levels.why: Interest rates change what families pay on loans and earn on savings.

levels.headline: Bank of England likely to raise interest rates on Thursday
levels.body:
The Bank of England will announce a decision on interest rates on Thursday, and it is expected to raise the rate from 3.75% to 4%. Almost everyone who follows money markets thinks this will happen.
The Bank wants prices to rise slowly, by about 2% a year. But prices rose 3.5% in the year to September, which is faster than experts thought. Energy is more expensive because of the conflict involving Iran, and ships are finding it hard to use a key oil route called the Strait of Hormuz. Shops, cafes and other services are also charging more.
The Bank puts rates up to make borrowing costlier, so people spend less and price rises slow. Some home loans already cost more. Five-year fixed deals reached about 5% in September, the highest for nearly two years.
levels.why: Rates change how much families pay on loans and how much they earn on savings.

levels.headline: The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates this week
levels.body:
The Bank of England will say on Thursday whether it will change interest rates. Nearly everyone expects it to raise them from 3.75% to 4%. Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow, or get paid when you save.
Why would it do this? Prices are going up faster than it wants. This is called inflation. Last year, a basket of everyday items cost 100 pounds. Now it costs a bit more than 103 pounds, because prices rose 3.5%. The Bank wants a rise of only 2%. Energy costs more because of the conflict involving Iran, and oil ships struggle to use a key sea route.
When borrowing costs more, people spend less, and that helps slow price rises. But it also means bigger bills for people paying off a home. Mortgage deals of five years now cost about 5%.
levels.why: It could change monthly payments for families with a mortgage, and what savers earn.

levels.headline: Bank of England likely to make borrowing dearer this week
levels.body:
The Bank of England is a special bank that helps look after the country's money. On Thursday it will say whether it is changing the interest rate. Most people think it will go up from 3.75% to 4%.
Interest rate means the price of borrowing money. If you borrow, you pay a bit extra back. The Bank is thinking about this because prices are rising too fast. A sweet that cost one pound last year might cost one pound and three pence now. The Bank would like prices to go up much more slowly. Fuel and energy cost more because of a war, and that pushes up many other prices too.
A higher rate makes people think harder before spending. That helps slow prices. But families with a loan for their home may have to pay more each month.
levels.why: It could change what families pay each month on home loans.

levels.headline: The Bank of England might make borrowing cost more
levels.body:
There is a big bank in Britain called the Bank of England. It helps keep prices steady. This week it may make one thing cost more. That thing is borrowing money.
When you borrow, you pay back a little extra. That extra is called interest. Think of borrowing a toy from a friend and giving back the toy plus a sticker as a thank you. The Bank may make that sticker bigger.
Why? Prices in the shops are going up too fast. A snack that cost one pound last year costs a few pence more now. The Bank wants prices to stay calm. Making borrowing cost more makes grown-ups spend less, and that can help prices stop climbing. The grown-ups decide on Thursday.
levels.why: Grown-ups with a home loan may have to pay a bit more every month.

headline: S&P 500 closed down 1.82% on Friday as tech shares were dumped, with Monday's session still in progress

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 of the largest companies listed in the United States.
A stock index dominated by technology companies.
An index of 30 large US companies.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closed down 1.82% on Friday as tech shares were dumped, with Monday's session still in progress
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down on Friday 30 October, the last completed trading session, falling 1.82% to 7,580.07. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 572.25 points, or 1.09%, to finish at 51,770.31, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86% to 25,437.00, its worst day since June, according to CNBC.
The Dow held up better because investors moved into defensive sectors such as consumer staples and healthcare, with Walmart and Coca-Cola each rising more than 1%. For October as a whole the Nasdaq fell 5.3%, its steepest monthly drop since March 2025, the S&P 500 fell 0.9% and the Dow gained 1.7%.
Monday's session is still under way. CNBC reported stocks higher in morning trading, with the S&P 500 up about 0.6% and the Nasdaq up about 0.7%, as oil prices tumbled ahead of Tuesday's US midterm elections.
levels.why: Share prices drive pensions, savings and business confidence on both sides of the Atlantic.

levels.headline: Wall Street falls on Friday as tech shares are sold off; Monday trading still under way
levels.body:
US stocks fell sharply on Friday 30 October, the latest completed session. The S&P 500 closed down 1.82% at 7,580.07. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.09%, or 572.25 points, to 51,770.31, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 2.86% to 25,437.00, its worst day since June.
The Dow fell less than the other two indexes because investors bought defensive shares, such as supermarkets and healthcare firms. Walmart and Coca-Cola each rose by more than 1%. Over the whole of October the Nasdaq lost 5.3%, its biggest monthly fall since March 2025. The S&P 500 slipped 0.9%, while the Dow gained 1.7%.
Trading on Monday has not finished. In the morning the S&P 500 was about 0.6% higher and the Nasdaq about 0.7% higher, helped by a sharp drop in oil prices before the US midterm elections.
levels.why: Falling share prices can reduce the value of pensions and make firms more cautious about investing.

levels.headline: US shares fall sharply on Friday as investors sell technology firms
levels.body:
The S&P 500, a measure of 500 big US companies, closed down on Friday 30 October. It fell 1.82% to 7,580.07. The Dow Jones index, which tracks 30 large firms, dropped 1.09% to 51,770.31. The Nasdaq, which has many technology companies, fell 2.86% to 25,437.00, its worst day since June.
The Dow fell by less because investors moved money into steadier businesses such as food and healthcare. Walmart and Coca-Cola both rose by more than 1%. Across October, the Nasdaq lost 5.3%, its largest monthly fall since March 2025. The S&P 500 lost 0.9% and the Dow rose 1.7%.
Monday's trading is still going on. In the morning, the S&P 500 was up about 0.6% and the Nasdaq about 0.7%, as the oil price dropped ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections in the United States.
levels.why: What happens to US shares often affects UK investments and pensions too.

levels.headline: Wall Street ends Friday lower after a tech sell-off
levels.body:
US share prices fell sharply on Friday 30 October, the last full day of trading. The S&P 500, which follows 500 big companies, closed down 1.82% at 7,580.07. The Dow Jones, which follows 30 large companies, fell 1.09% to 51,770.31. The Nasdaq, packed with technology firms, dropped 2.86% to 25,437.00. That was its worst day since June.
The Dow did better because investors bought shares in firms that sell everyday things, such as Walmart and Coca-Cola, which both rose by more than 1%. Over the whole of October, the Nasdaq lost 5.3%, the S&P 500 lost 0.9% and the Dow gained 1.7%.
Monday's trading has not finished yet. By the morning, the S&P 500 was up about 0.6% and the Nasdaq up about 0.7%, after oil prices fell ahead of the US elections.
levels.why: Share prices can affect pensions and how confident businesses feel.

levels.headline: US shares drop on Friday as people sell tech companies
levels.body:
On Friday 30 October, share prices in the United States fell a lot. The S&P 500 is a list of 500 big companies, and its value went down 1.82% to 7,580.07. The Dow Jones, a list of 30 large companies, fell 1.09% to 51,770.31. The Nasdaq, which has many technology companies, fell 2.86% to 25,437.00. That was its worst day since June.
Some shares did better. Walmart and Coca-Cola both rose by more than 1%, because people see them as safer. Over the whole month of October, the Nasdaq lost 5.3%, the S&P 500 lost 0.9% and the Dow gained 1.7%.
Monday is not over yet. This morning the S&P 500 was up about 0.6% and the Nasdaq about 0.7%. The price of oil had dropped before the American elections on Tuesday.
levels.why: Many people's pensions are invested in shares, so big falls can matter to them.

levels.headline: American share prices fell sharply on Friday
levels.body:
Share prices in the United States fell a lot on Friday 30 October, the last full day of trading. Many investors sold shares in technology companies. When lots of people sell, prices go down.
There are lists, called indexes, that show how groups of companies are doing. The S&P 500, which follows 500 big firms, closed down 1.82% at 7,580.07. The Dow Jones, which follows 30 large firms, fell 1.09% to 51,770.31. The Nasdaq, which has many technology firms, fell 2.86% to 25,437.00, its worst day since June.
Monday's trading is not over yet. In the morning, prices were rising a little. The S&P 500 was up about 0.6% and the Nasdaq about 0.7%, after oil got cheaper ahead of the US elections.
levels.why: Falling share prices can change the value of pensions and savings.

levels.headline: American shares fell sharply on Friday
levels.body:
A share is a small piece of a company. When many people sell shares, prices fall. That happened in the United States on Friday 30 October. People sold a lot of shares in technology companies.
There are lists, called indexes, that show how groups of companies are doing. The S&P 500 follows 500 big companies. On Friday it fell 1.82% to 7,580.07. The Dow Jones follows 30 big companies, and it fell 1.09% to 51,770.31. The Nasdaq follows many technology firms, and it fell 2.86% to 25,437.00. That was its worst day since June.

levels.why: Falling share prices can change the value of pensions and savings.

levels.headline: Share prices fell a lot in America on Friday
levels.body:
A company can be split into tiny pieces called shares. People buy and sell them. When lots of people sell, the price goes down. On Friday 30 October, that happened to many companies in America, especially ones that make technology.
There are scoreboards called indexes. They show how groups of companies are doing. One is the S&P 500, which follows 500 big companies. It went down 1.82% on Friday, to 7,580.07. The Dow Jones follows 30 big firms. It went down 1.09% to 51,770.31. The Nasdaq follows many technology firms. It went down 2.86% to 25,437.00. That was its worst day since June.
Today, Monday, the day is not over. This morning prices were up a little. The S&P 500 was up about 0.6%.
levels.why: Grown-ups' pensions are often kept in shares, so big falls can matter.

levels.headline: Many shares got cheaper in America on Friday
levels.body:
Imagine a big cake shared between lots of people. A share is one tiny slice of a company. On Friday, 30 October, many people in America sold their slices of technology companies. When many people sell, the price of a slice goes down.
There are scoreboards for company slices. They are called the S&P 500, the Dow Jones and the Nasdaq. On Friday all three went down. The Nasdaq went down the most, by 2.86%. That was its worst day since June. The S&P 500 went down 1.82%. The Dow went down 1.09%.
The week has started again now. On Monday morning, prices were going up a little bit. The S&P 500 was up about 0.6%. Today is not finished, so we do not know how it will end.
levels.why: Some grown-ups save for later by owning slices of companies, so these changes matter to them.

levels.headline: Shares went down on Friday
levels.body:
Companies sell tiny pieces of themselves. These pieces are called shares. People buy them, like collecting stickers, and hope they become worth more. Sometimes the price goes up. Sometimes it goes down.
On Friday, many people in America sold shares in computer and technology companies. So the prices went down. A scoreboard called the S&P 500 went down by about two in every hundred. The Nasdaq, which has lots of technology companies, went down by nearly three in every hundred. The Dow went down by one in every hundred.
On Monday, the prices started going up again, just a little. The day is not over, so we cannot say how it will end. Shares can go up and down quickly.
levels.why: Grown-ups put money into shares, so these ups and downs matter to them.

headline: Healey's Budget raises bank tax and avoids income tax rises, but OBR cuts 2027 growth forecast to 1%

terms.meaning: The gap between the government's planned borrowing and the limit set by its own fiscal rules.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent body that forecasts the economy and public finances.
Bonds the UK government sells to borrow money.

levels.headline: Healey's Budget raises bank tax and avoids income tax rises, but OBR cuts 2027 growth forecast to 1%
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey's Budget on 28 October left the headline rates of income tax, National Insurance and VAT unchanged, with the government saying there would be no tax rises on wages or dividends. Revenue instead came from banks, gambling firms and vape shops, with the bank surcharge rising by 3 points to 6%. Targeted tax measures are due to raise £6.6 billion a year by 2030-31.
The Office for Budget Responsibility estimated headroom against the stability rule at around £15 billion, lower than a year earlier, with much of the squeeze caused by higher debt interest from rising gilt yields. It cut its 2027 growth forecast to 1% from 1.6%, citing the economic impact of the Iran war.
Markets reacted broadly positively. The 10-year gilt yield was about 2 basis points lower at 5.323% during the speech. Borrowing is forecast to fall from 4.2% of GDP in 2026-27 to 1.8% in 2031-32.
levels.why: The Budget sets taxes and spending for millions of households and businesses.

levels.headline: Budget avoids income tax rises, taxes banks and gambling, as growth forecast is cut
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey's Budget on 28 October did not raise the headline rates of income tax, National Insurance or VAT. He said there would be no tax rises on wages or dividends. The extra money came mainly from banks, gambling businesses and vape shops, with the bank surcharge going up by 3 points to 6%. These targeted measures should raise £6.6 billion a year by 2030-31.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent forecaster, said the government has about £15 billion of headroom against its main borrowing rule. That is less than last year, partly because the cost of servicing debt has grown as gilt yields rose. It also cut its 2027 growth forecast to 1% from 1.6%, citing the Iran war.
Markets responded broadly positively, and the 10-year gilt yield dipped slightly to about 5.32%.
levels.why: Taxes and the state of public finances affect jobs, prices and public services.

levels.headline: Healey's Budget leaves main tax rates alone but raises tax on banks and gambling
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey presented his Budget on 28 October. He did not raise the main rates of income tax, National Insurance or VAT, and said there would be no tax rises on wages or dividends. Instead, banks, gambling companies and vape shops will pay more. The extra tax on banks goes up by 3 points to 6%. Together, such measures should bring in £6.6 billion a year by 2030-31.
The independent Office for Budget Responsibility said the government has around £15 billion of room against its own borrowing rule. That is smaller than last year, partly because the government now pays more interest on its debts. The office also cut its growth forecast for 2027 to 1% from 1.6%, blaming the Iran war.
Financial markets reacted fairly calmly, and the cost of government borrowing edged down.
levels.why: The Budget affects tax bills and how confident businesses feel.

levels.headline: Budget keeps income tax and VAT rates the same but makes banks pay more
levels.body:
On 28 October the Chancellor, John Healey, set out the Budget. The main rates of income tax, National Insurance and VAT stay the same, and he said wages and dividends would not be taxed more. To raise money, banks, gambling firms and vape shops will pay extra tax. Banks' extra tax goes up from 3% to 6%. Plans like these should raise £6.6 billion a year by 2030-31.
The government's own forecasters, the Office for Budget Responsibility, said it has about £15 billion of space before it breaks its borrowing rules. That is less than last year, because the interest it pays on its debts has risen. They also lowered their 2027 growth forecast to 1%, from 1.6%, because of the Iran war.
Markets took the news calmly. The cost of government borrowing dipped slightly.
levels.why: Decisions in the Budget shape what people pay in tax and what the government can afford.

levels.headline: The Budget did not raise income tax, but banks and gambling firms will pay more
levels.body:
On 28 October the Chancellor, John Healey, shared the government's plan for taxes and spending. This is called the Budget. He did not raise the main taxes that most people pay: income tax, National Insurance and VAT. He said wages would not be taxed more.
Instead, some businesses will pay more. Banks will pay a bigger extra tax, rising from 3% to 6%. Gambling firms and vape shops will pay more too. The government hopes to raise £6.6 billion a year by 2030-31.
A group called the Office for Budget Responsibility checks the government's sums. It said there is about £15 billion of spare room before the government breaks its own rules on borrowing. That is less than last year, because interest on the government's debt has gone up. The group also expects the economy to grow by 1% in 2027, down from 1.6%, because of the Iran war.
levels.why: It shows how the government plans to pay for schools, hospitals and more.

levels.headline: The Budget keeps main taxes the same but makes banks and gambling firms pay more

On 28 October the Chancellor, John Healey, set out the government's plan for taxes and spending. This is called the Budget. The main taxes that most people pay stay at the same rates. These are income tax, National Insurance and VAT. He said wages and dividends would not be taxed more.

levels.headline: The Chancellor kept main taxes the same but asked banks to pay more
levels.body:
A Budget is a yearly plan that says how much tax the government will collect and how it will spend it. The Chancellor is the minister in charge of that money. His name is John Healey, and he gave the Budget on 28 October.
He did not raise the taxes most people pay, such as income tax or VAT. Instead, banks, gambling firms and vape shops will pay more. Banks will pay a bigger extra tax, going from 3% to 6%. The government hopes this will raise about £6.6 billion a year by 2030-31.
A team of experts checks the government's sums. They said the government has some spare room in its borrowing plans, but less than last year. This is because the government pays more interest on money it has borrowed. They also think the economy will grow more slowly in 2027, because of the war involving Iran.
levels.why: The Budget affects the taxes families pay and the services they use.

levels.headline: The government said who will pay more tax
levels.body:
Every year, the government says how it will get money and how it will spend it. This is called the Budget. The person in charge of the money is called the Chancellor. This year it is John Healey, and he spoke on 28 October.
He did not make the main taxes bigger for ordinary workers. Instead, banks, gambling companies and vape shops will pay more. The government hopes this will bring in about £6.6 billion each year by 2030-31. That is a very large amount of money.
The government also borrows money, a bit like a family taking out a loan. A group of experts looked at the sums. They said there is still some room to borrow, but not as much as before. They also think the country's money-making will grow slower next year, because of a war involving Iran.
levels.why: It decides how much tax people pay and what the government can afford to do.

levels.headline: The Chancellor told the country how the government will get its money
levels.body:
The government needs money for schools, hospitals and roads. It gets that money from taxes. Once a year, a person called the Chancellor explains the plan. The Chancellor is John Healey, and he did it on 28 October.
Taxes are money people and businesses pay to the government. He did not make the main taxes bigger for workers. But banks will pay more. So will gambling companies and shops that sell vapes. The government thinks this could bring in about £6.6 billion each year in a few years' time.
Experts also checked the plan. They said the government is not borrowing too much, but it has less spare room than last year. They also think the country will earn a little less than hoped next year. The war involving Iran is one reason.
levels.why: The plan decides how much tax people pay and how much the government can spend.

levels.headline: The government shared its plan for money
levels.body:
A government is a bit like a very big family. It has money coming in and money going out. The money coming in is called tax. People and companies pay tax. Then the government spends it on things like schools and hospitals.
Once a year, the person in charge of the money tells everyone the plan. The job is called the Chancellor, and this one is John Healey. He told everyone on 28 October. He did not ask most workers to pay more. But banks have to pay more. Companies that run gambling and shops that sell vapes have to pay more too.
Some experts checked the plan. They said it was fine, but there is not much spare room. They think the country may grow a bit slower next year, because of a war far away.
levels.why: It decides how much grown-ups pay in tax and what the country can spend.

headline: Votes at 16 bill enters House of Lords committee stage, with overseas and crypto donations curbed

terms.meaning: The part of a bill's journey where members examine it line by line and can propose changes.
Being added to the official list of people who can vote.
The second chamber of Parliament, which examines and can amend bills.

levels.headline: Votes at 16 bill enters House of Lords committee stage, with overseas and crypto donations curbed
levels.body:
The Representation of the People Bill has entered its committee stage in the House of Lords, where peers will examine its measures in detail, according to a government post published on 2 November. The bill would give 16 and 17-year-olds the right to vote in all elections across the UK.
It would also lower the age at which people can register to vote to 14, so that young people can be fully registered for an election that falls close to their 16th birthday. A government press release put the number of 16 and 17-year-olds affected at about 1.7 million.
On political finance, the bill sets a cap of £100,000 a year on donations from overseas electors and bans political donations made in crypto assets. The search found no report of any votes in the Lords committee so far, so the final shape of these measures is not yet settled.
levels.why: It could change who gets a say in every UK election and how parties are funded.

levels.headline: Votes at 16 bill reaches House of Lords committee stage
levels.body:
The Representation of the People Bill has reached committee stage in the House of Lords, the government said on 2 November. At this stage peers examine the bill in detail and can propose changes. The bill would let 16 and 17-year-olds vote in every UK election, which the government says would affect about 1.7 million young people.
It would also lower the age for registering to vote to 14. This would allow young people to be fully registered before an election that falls close to their 16th birthday.
The bill also tightens rules on political money. Donations from overseas electors would be capped at £100,000 a year, and donations made in crypto assets would be banned. No results from votes in the Lords committee have been reported yet, so the details could still change as the bill continues through Parliament.
levels.why: Changing the voting age and donation rules would alter who takes part in politics.

levels.headline: Plan to let 16-year-olds vote across the UK moves to a new stage in the Lords
levels.body:
A bill that would let 16 and 17-year-olds vote in all UK elections has reached the committee stage in the House of Lords. The government announced this on 2 November. In committee, members of the Lords go through a bill line by line and can suggest changes. The government says around 1.7 million young people would gain the vote.
The Representation of the People Bill would also lower the age for joining the electoral register to 14. That means a young person could be on the list in time to vote soon after turning 16.
There are new rules on money in politics too. People living abroad who are on the voting register could give no more than £100,000 a year, and donations in cryptocurrencies would be banned. No votes from the Lords have been reported yet.
levels.why: It could change who can vote and how political parties raise money.

levels.headline: Bill giving 16-year-olds the vote moves forward in the House of Lords
levels.body:
A bill that would give 16 and 17-year-olds the vote in every UK election has now reached the House of Lords committee stage. The government said so on 2 November. At this stage, members of the Lords study the bill closely and can suggest changes. About 1.7 million young people would be able to vote if it becomes law.
The bill would also let people sign up to the voting list from the age of 14. That way, someone who turns 16 close to an election can already be on the list.
There are changes to money in politics too. Voters living abroad could give a party no more than £100,000 in a year. Gifts made using cryptocurrency, a type of digital money, would be banned. No votes have been reported yet.
levels.why: It affects who can have a say in elections and how parties are paid for.

levels.headline: A bill to let 16-year-olds vote has reached the House of Lords
levels.body:
The government wants 16 and 17-year-olds to be able to vote in every election in the UK. A new law called the Representation of the People Bill would do this. On 2 November, the government said the bill had reached a new stage in the House of Lords. The Lords are a group of people who check new laws. In this stage, they go through the bill carefully and can suggest changes.
About 1.7 million young people would be able to vote. The bill would also let young people be put on the voting list at 14. Then they are ready to vote soon after turning 16.
It also changes rules about money. Someone living abroad could give a party no more than £100,000 a year. Gifts of crypto money would be banned.
levels.why: It could change who gets to vote in future elections.

levels.headline: Plan to let 16-year-olds vote reaches the House of Lords
levels.body:
The government wants 16 and 17-year-olds to be able to vote in every election in the UK. A bill, which is a plan for a new law, would make this happen. On 2 November, the government said the bill had reached the House of Lords committee stage. This is where members of the Lords go through the bill line by line and can suggest changes.
About 1.7 million young people would be able to vote. People could also be added to the voting list at 14, so they are ready when they turn 16.
The bill also changes the rules on money in politics. Voters living abroad could give a party no more than £100,000 a year. Gifts in crypto, a type of digital money, would be banned.
levels.why: It could change who gets to vote in future elections.

levels.headline: The House of Lords is looking at a plan to let 16-year-olds vote
levels.body:
In the UK, you must be 18 to vote in most elections now. The government wants to change that. A new bill would let people vote from 16. A bill is a plan for a new law. Both parts of Parliament must agree to it before it becomes law.
On 2 November, the bill reached the House of Lords. The Lords check new laws and can ask for changes. About 1.7 million young people aged 16 and 17 would be able to vote. People could also join the voting list at 14, so they are ready when they turn 16.
The bill also deals with money in politics. A person living abroad could give a party no more than £100,000 a year. Gifts made in crypto, a kind of online money, would not be allowed.
levels.why: It could mean teenagers get a say on who runs the country.

levels.headline: Plans to let 16-year-olds vote move on in Parliament
levels.body:
Voting is how people choose who runs the country. Right now, you usually have to be 18 to vote. A new plan would change this so that people can vote at 16. The plan is written down in a bill. A bill becomes a law only if Parliament says yes.
On 2 November, the bill got to a new step. It is in the House of Lords, where people check new laws and can ask for changes. About 1.7 million teenagers aged 16 and 17 would get to vote if it passes.
The bill also says people can sign up to the voting list when they are 14. That helps them be ready. It also limits big gifts of money to political parties from people living abroad. It bans gifts of online crypto money.
levels.why: It could let teenagers choose who makes the rules.

levels.headline: A plan to let teenagers vote is moving through Parliament
levels.body:
Voting means choosing who will make the rules for a country. Right now, only people who are 18 or older can vote in most elections. A new plan would let 16-year-olds vote too. That is about 1.7 million teenagers.
A plan for a new law is called a bill. A bill has to be checked by lots of people before it can become a law. On 2 November, this bill got to a part of Parliament called the House of Lords. The Lords read it carefully and can ask for changes, like a teacher checking homework.
The bill would also let young people join the voting list at 14. It also says that very big gifts of money to political parties must be limited.
levels.why: It could give teenagers a voice in choosing leaders.

levels.headline: Grown-ups are talking about letting teenagers vote
levels.body:
Voting is when people choose who will be in charge. In Britain, you have to be 18 to vote at the moment. Some grown-ups want to change that. They want 16-year-olds to be able to vote too.
To change a rule like that, they need a new law. A plan for a new law is called a bill. Lots of grown-ups have to read the bill and check it. On 2 November, some of them in a place called the House of Lords started to read this bill very carefully. It is like when a teacher checks your work and says what could be better.
If the plan becomes a law, about one and a half million teenagers could vote. We do not know yet if it will happen.
levels.why: It might mean teenagers can help pick who is in charge.

headline: UK government borrowing costs stay near 2007 highs as five-year mortgage rates reach 5%

terms.meaning: The return investors get from holding a UK government bond, which rises when the price of the bond falls and shows the cost of government borrowing.
A loan taken out to buy a home.
An interest rate that stays the same for an agreed number of years.

levels.headline: UK government borrowing costs stay near 2007 highs as five-year mortgage rates reach 5%
levels.body:
The cost of UK government borrowing remains close to its highest level in almost two decades. The 10-year gilt yield peaked at about 5.5% on 1 October, its highest since July 2007, and the 30-year yield reached 6%. Since then, the 10-year yield has traded roughly between 5.3% and 5.4%, according to Trading Economics.
Higher gilt yields push up the interest the government pays on its debt, and they also influence loan costs across the economy. Five-year fixed mortgage rates reached 5% in September, the highest since October 2023. Public sector net borrowing was £24.5 billion in September, above forecasts.
The Bank of England is expected to raise Bank Rate to 4% on 5 November, and the Office for Budget Responsibility said higher debt interest had squeezed the Chancellor's headroom. Inflation rose to 3.5% in September.
levels.why: Government borrowing costs feed into mortgages, taxes and what the Chancellor can afford.

levels.headline: UK government borrowing costs stay high as mortgage rates reach 5%
levels.body:
The cost for the UK government to borrow money is still close to its highest in almost 20 years. The 10-year gilt yield, which shows that cost, peaked at about 5.5% on 1 October, the highest since July 2007. The 30-year yield touched 6%. Since then, the 10-year yield has stayed between about 5.3% and 5.4%, Trading Economics reports.
Higher gilt yields mean the government pays more interest on its debts, and they also push up borrowing costs for households and firms. Five-year fixed mortgage rates reached 5% in September, the highest since October 2023. In September, the government borrowed £24.5 billion, more than forecast.
The Bank of England is expected to raise Bank Rate to 4% on 5 November. The Budget watchdog said higher debt interest had cut the Chancellor's room for manoeuvre.
levels.why: High borrowing costs affect mortgages and limit what the government can spend.

levels.headline: The cost of government borrowing stays near a 19-year high
levels.body:
The cost of government borrowing in the UK is still close to its highest in almost 20 years. Gilts are bonds that the government sells to borrow money. The yield on a 10-year gilt reached about 5.5% on 1 October, the highest since July 2007. The yield on 30-year gilts hit 6%. Since then, the 10-year figure has stayed at about 5.3% to 5.4%.
A higher yield means the government pays more interest on what it owes. It also tends to push up the cost of other loans. Typical five-year fixed mortgage rates reached 5% in September, the highest since October 2023. The government also borrowed £24.5 billion in September, more than expected.
The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates to 4% on 5 November.
levels.why: It can mean higher mortgage costs and less money for public services.

levels.headline: Government borrowing costs stay high, and mortgage rates are up
levels.body:
It still costs the UK government a lot to borrow money. The government borrows by selling bonds called gilts. The yield on a 10-year gilt is the interest rate it effectively pays. On 1 October it reached about 5.5%, the highest since July 2007. For 30-year gilts it hit 6%. Since then the 10-year yield has stayed between about 5.3% and 5.4%.
When the government pays more interest, it has less to spend on other things. High yields also push up the cost of other loans. Five-year fixed mortgages reached 5% in September, the highest since October 2023. The government also borrowed £24.5 billion in September, which was more than experts expected.
The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates to 4% on 5 November.
levels.why: It affects mortgage costs and how much the government can spend.

levels.headline: It costs the government a lot to borrow, and mortgages cost more too
levels.body:
Like a family, the government sometimes borrows money. It does this by selling bonds called gilts. People who buy them are paid interest. At the start of October, the interest on a 10-year gilt reached about 5.5%. That was the highest since 2007. It has since eased slightly to about 5.3% or 5.4%.
When the government pays more interest, it has less left for other things, such as schools and hospitals. High interest rates for the government also tend to push up the cost of loans for everyone else. In September, a typical five-year fixed mortgage cost about 5%. That was the highest since October 2023.
The government also borrowed £24.5 billion in September, which was more than experts predicted.
levels.why: It can mean higher home loan costs and less money for public services.

levels.headline: It costs the UK government more to borrow, and home loans cost more too
levels.body:
The UK government often borrows money by selling bonds called gilts. It pays interest to the people who buy them. On 1 October, the interest on a 10-year gilt reached about 5.5%, the highest since 2007. It has since eased a little, to about 5.3% or 5.4%.
This matters in two ways. First, when the government pays more interest, it has less left to spend on things like schools and hospitals. Second, high rates for the government tend to push up the cost of other loans. In September, a mortgage fixed for five years cost about 5%. That was the highest since October 2023.
The government also borrowed £24.5 billion in September, which was more than experts predicted.
levels.why: It affects the cost of mortgages and how much the government can spend.

levels.headline: Borrowing money is still expensive for the government and for home buyers
levels.body:
Sometimes the government needs more money than it has. So it borrows, by selling bonds called gilts. It pays interest to the people who buy them. Early in October, the interest on a 10-year gilt reached about 5.5%. That was the highest since 2007. It has dropped a little since, to about 5.3% or 5.4%.
This matters because paying more interest leaves less for schools and hospitals. It also affects families. A mortgage is a loan to buy a home, and a deal fixed for five years reached about 5% in September. That was the highest in nearly two years.
The government also borrowed £24.5 billion in September, more than experts had guessed.
levels.why: It affects home loans and how much the government can spend.

levels.headline: The government and home buyers are paying more to borrow
levels.body:
To borrow means to take money now and pay it back later with extra. The extra is called interest. The government borrows too. It sells bonds called gilts, and the people who buy them get interest. In October, the interest reached about 5.5% a year for a 10-year gilt. That is the highest since 2007. It has fallen a bit since then.
When the government pays more interest, it has less left to spend on things like schools. Families are affected too. A mortgage is a big loan to buy a home. In September, a mortgage with a rate fixed for five years cost about 5%, the highest in almost two years.
The government also borrowed £24.5 billion in September, more than people thought.
levels.why: It affects home loans and what the government can spend.

levels.headline: Borrowing money has become more costly
levels.body:
If you borrow a toy from a friend, you give it back. If you borrow money, you give back the money and a bit extra. The extra is called interest. The government borrows money too, to pay for schools and hospitals. The bit extra it pays has become big. In October it was about 5.5% a year, the highest since 2007.
That is a problem because the government then has less money for other things. It is also a problem for grown-ups who want to buy a home. They borrow a big amount, called a mortgage. In September, the extra on a mortgage fixed for five years was about 5% a year. That is the highest in nearly two years.
The government borrowed more than people expected last month too.
levels.why: It means grown-ups pay more for loans, and the government has less to spend.

levels.headline: Borrowing money costs more than before
levels.body:
When you borrow something, you give it back later. When grown-ups borrow money, they give back a bit extra too. The extra is called interest. Think of it like paying a small fee for borrowing a friend's bike. Right now the fee is quite big. It is the biggest it has been for a long time.
Even the government has to pay it. The government borrows money to pay for schools, roads and hospitals. If it pays a big fee, it has less left to spend on those things.
Families pay it too. Grown-ups who borrow money to buy a house pay about five extra pounds for every hundred pounds borrowed, each year. That is more than they used to.
levels.why: Grown-ups who borrow pay more, and so does the government.

headline: Oil falls more than 7% on hopes of a diplomatic deal with Iran, but Brent stays above $100

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil.
Extra price added to a commodity because traders fear something could go wrong.
West Texas Intermediate, the main US benchmark price for oil.

levels.headline: Oil falls more than 7% on hopes of a diplomatic deal with Iran, but Brent stays above $100
levels.body:
Oil prices fell sharply on Monday 2 November on hopes of a diplomatic deal between the United States and Iran. By 12:11 p.m. Eastern Time, Brent crude futures were down 7.7% at $104.66 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate was down 7.3% at $96.50, CNBC reported.
TD Securities said much of the recent rise in prices had been a risk premium, meaning traders had added extra cost in case of escalation. Trading Economics listed Brent at about $105.86, so exact quotes differ between sources.
The fall eased worries about inflation in other markets, and gold rebounded after hitting a one-year low. Prices have been lifted by the Iran conflict and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. Oil is a main driver of fuel and energy bills, which have pushed inflation higher in the US, the UK and Europe. Brent is still well above $100.
levels.why: Oil prices feed straight into petrol, heating bills and inflation.

levels.headline: Oil drops more than 7% on hopes for talks between the US and Iran
levels.body:
The price of oil fell sharply on Monday 2 November because of hopes that the United States and Iran can reach a diplomatic deal. By midday in New York, Brent crude was down 7.7% at $104.66 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate fell 7.3% to $96.50, according to CNBC.
TD Securities said much of the recent rise in prices was a risk premium, which means extra cost added by traders who feared things could get worse. Trading Economics listed Brent at about $105.86, so quotes vary slightly.
The drop eased fears about inflation elsewhere in the markets, and gold rose after reaching a one-year low. The price of oil has been pushed up by the Iran conflict and problems for shipping near the Strait of Hormuz. Brent remains above $100.
levels.why: Falling oil could eventually ease pressure on fuel and energy bills.

levels.headline: Oil prices tumble as hopes grow of a deal with Iran
levels.body:
The price of oil fell by more than 7% on Monday 2 November, as hopes grew of a diplomatic deal between the United States and Iran. By midday in New York, Brent crude, the main international price, had fallen 7.7% to $104.66 a barrel. The main US price, called West Texas Intermediate, fell 7.3% to $96.50.
An analyst at TD Securities said much of the recent rise was a risk premium. That is the extra price traders add when they fear that something could go wrong. Prices differ slightly between sources, and one listed Brent at about $105.86.
The fall eased worries about inflation, and gold rebounded from a one-year low. Oil has been expensive because of the Iran conflict and disruption near the Strait of Hormuz. Brent is still above $100.
levels.why: The price of oil affects petrol, heating and the cost of many goods.

levels.headline: Oil prices fall sharply on hopes of a US and Iran deal
levels.body:
Oil became much cheaper on Monday 2 November. The price fell by more than 7% because people hope the United States and Iran can agree a deal. By midday in New York, Brent crude, the main world price, was down 7.7% at $104.66 a barrel. The main American price fell 7.3% to $96.50.
A bank called TD Securities said a lot of the recent rise was a risk premium. This is extra money added to the price because traders were afraid things could get worse, such as more fighting. Different sources give slightly different prices.
The fall eased fears about prices rising across the economy. Oil has been dear because of the conflict involving Iran and problems for ships near the Strait of Hormuz. It is still above $100 a barrel.
levels.why: Oil prices affect what people pay for petrol and energy.

levels.headline: Oil gets much cheaper as people hope for peace talks with Iran
levels.body:
The price of oil fell by more than 7% on Monday 2 November. People hope the United States and Iran can make a deal without more fighting. By midday in New York, Brent crude, the main world price, was $104.66 a barrel, down 7.7%. The main American price was $96.50, down 7.3%.
A bank said much of the earlier rise came from fear. When traders fear that something bad might happen, they pay extra for oil in case it becomes scarce. This extra is called a risk premium. Now there is hope for talks, so some of it has gone.
The drop eased worries about rising prices. Oil has been dear because of the conflict involving Iran and problems for ships near a narrow route called the Strait of Hormuz. It is still above $100.
levels.why: Cheaper oil can help bring down petrol and energy costs.

levels.headline: Oil gets much cheaper on hopes of a US and Iran deal
levels.body:
The price of oil fell by more than 7% on Monday 2 November. People hope that the United States and Iran can reach a deal by talking, without more fighting. By midday in New York, a barrel of Brent oil, the main world kind, cost $104.66. That was down 7.7%. The main American kind fell 7.3% to $96.50.
A bank called TD Securities said a lot of the earlier rise came from fear. When traders fear things could get worse, they pay extra for oil, just in case. That extra is called a risk premium. Some of it has now gone.
Oil is still dear. It costs more because of the conflict involving Iran and trouble for ships using the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow oil route. It is still above $100.
levels.why: Cheaper oil can help lower petrol and energy costs.

levels.headline: Oil prices fell a lot because people hope for peace talks
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid dug from the ground. It is used to make petrol, diesel and many other things. On Monday 2 November, the price of oil fell by more than 7%. People hope that the United States and Iran can talk and make a deal, instead of fighting.
A barrel of Brent oil, the main world kind, cost $104.66 by midday in New York. That was 7.7% less than before. Traders had added extra to the price because they feared things might get worse. This extra is called a risk premium. Some of it has now gone.
Oil is still very dear. It has cost more because of the conflict involving Iran and trouble for ships near a narrow sea route. That route is called the Strait of Hormuz.
levels.why: Cheaper oil can lower petrol prices and help bring down the cost of living.

levels.headline: The price of oil dropped because people hope for peace
levels.body:
Oil comes from under the ground. We use it to make petrol for cars and fuel for lorries and planes. The price of oil goes up and down. On Monday 2 November, it dropped by more than 7%. This happened because people hope two countries, the United States and Iran, will talk instead of fighting.
One barrel of the main kind of oil cost about $105 by midday in New York. That is less than before, but it is still a lot. Before the drop, traders were scared that things would get worse. When people are scared, they will pay more for oil, just in case. That extra cost is now smaller.
Oil is expensive because of fighting involving Iran, and because ships find it hard to use a narrow sea route.
levels.why: It can change how much grown-ups pay for petrol and heating.

levels.headline: Oil got cheaper because people hope for peace
levels.body:
Oil comes from deep under the ground. People use it to make petrol for cars and fuel for lorries and planes. Oil costs more when it is hard to get. It costs less when it is easy to get. On Monday 2 November, the price dropped a lot. It fell by more than seven in every hundred.
This happened because two countries, the United States and Iran, might start talking. Before, people were worried that there would be more fighting. That would make oil harder to get. So they paid extra, just in case. Now they are less worried.
Oil still costs a lot. One barrel costs about $105. That is still more than $100. Grown-ups pay more for petrol when oil is dear.
levels.why: It can change how much grown-ups pay for petrol.

levels.headline: Oil costs less because people hope for peace
levels.body:
Oil comes from under the ground. It is used to make petrol for cars and buses. It is like a drink that machines need. When oil is hard to get, it costs more. When it is easy to get, it costs less.
On Monday, oil got cheaper. It dropped by a lot, more than seven pennies in every hundred pennies. This is because two countries, the United States and Iran, may start talking. Before, people worried that there would be fighting. They paid extra for oil in case it ran out. Now they worry less.
But oil is still expensive. A big barrel of it costs about one hundred and five dollars. When oil is dear, grown-ups pay more for petrol.
levels.why: It can change how much grown-ups pay to fill up the car.

headline: Fed holds rates at 3.75% to 4% as markets bet on a December rise with US inflation at 3.7%

terms.meaning: The central bank of the United States, which sets the country's main interest rate.
Favouring higher interest rates to fight inflation.
Inflation that leaves out volatile food and energy prices.

levels.headline: Fed holds rates at 3.75% to 4% as markets bet on a December rise with US inflation at 3.7%
levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on 28 October, keeping its target range at 3.75% to 4%. Two members dissented, including Lisa Cook. Chair Kevin Warsh disavowed any set course for rates but gave a strong signal that his lean is towards higher rates, CNBC reported.
The hold came after US consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August, with petrol a main driver. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, was 2.6%, up from 2.4%.
Markets are pricing a high chance of a rate rise in December, reported at between about 73% and 85% depending on the day. Barclays expects rises in December and January. Mr Warsh also announced the Fed would hold fewer rate-setting votes in future, skipping one in 2027 and two in 2028, while still meeting eight times a year.
levels.why: US interest rates influence borrowing costs, the dollar and markets around the world.

levels.headline: Fed holds interest rates and markets expect a rise in December
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, kept interest rates unchanged on 28 October at a range of 3.75% to 4%. Two members disagreed with the decision, including Lisa Cook. The Fed's chair, Kevin Warsh, said he did not have a fixed path in mind but strongly hinted he leans towards higher rates.
US inflation rose to 3.7% in September from 3.4% in August, with petrol prices a major cause. The measure that leaves out food and energy, called core inflation, rose to 2.6% from 2.4%.
Traders now think a rise in December is likely, with estimates ranging from about 73% to 85%. Barclays expects rises in December and January. Mr Warsh also said the Fed will hold fewer rate-setting votes in the next two years, though it will still meet eight times a year.
levels.why: The Fed's decisions affect mortgages, savings and exchange rates well beyond America.

levels.headline: US Federal Reserve holds rates, but a rise is expected in December
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve, America's central bank, left interest rates unchanged on 28 October, in a range of 3.75% to 4%. Two officials, including Lisa Cook, voted against. Chair Kevin Warsh said no path was set, but he strongly hinted that he leans towards higher rates.
US inflation went up to 3.7% in September, from 3.4% in August, mainly because petrol cost more. A measure that leaves out food and energy prices rose from 2.4% to 2.6%.
Financial traders now think a rise in rates in December is likely. Estimates of the chance range from about 73% to 85%. The bank Barclays expects increases in December and January. Mr Warsh also said the Fed will hold fewer votes on rates in future, though it will still meet eight times a year.
levels.why: What the Fed does can change borrowing costs around the world.

levels.headline: The US central bank keeps interest rates the same, but a rise may be coming
levels.body:
The US central bank, called the Federal Reserve, left its interest rate unchanged on 28 October, at between 3.75% and 4%. Two members of the committee disagreed. The chair, Kevin Warsh, said he had not decided what to do next, but he strongly hinted that he leans towards raising rates.
Prices in the US rose 3.7% in the year to September, up from 3.4% the month before. Petrol was a big reason. Prices excluding food and energy rose 2.6%, up from 2.4%.
Investors now think the Fed will probably raise rates in December. Estimates put the chance at between about 73% and 85%. One bank, Barclays, expects rises in both December and January. Mr Warsh also said the Fed will hold fewer decision votes in future. It will still meet eight times a year.
levels.why: US rates can affect loans and the value of currencies worldwide.

levels.headline: The US central bank kept rates the same but may raise them soon
levels.body:
The US has a central bank called the Federal Reserve, or the Fed. It sets the main interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. On 28 October it kept the rate the same, between 3.75% and 4%. Its boss, Kevin Warsh, said he had not decided what to do next. But he hinted he leans towards raising it.
He may do that because prices are going up faster. They rose 3.7% in the year to September. A month earlier, it was 3.4%. Petrol cost much more. Prices without food and energy rose 2.6%.
People who trade money now think the Fed will probably raise the rate in December. They put the chance at roughly 73% to 85%. The Fed will also vote on rates a bit less often in future years.
levels.why: It can change how much people and firms pay to borrow around the world.

levels.headline: America's central bank keeps rates the same but may raise them in December
levels.body:
America's central bank is called the Federal Reserve. It sets the main interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. On 28 October it left the rate at between 3.75% and 4%. Its chair, Kevin Warsh, said he had not decided what to do next, but hinted he leans towards raising it.
He may think that because prices in the US keep rising. They went up 3.7% in the year to September, up from 3.4% a month before. Petrol cost much more. Prices without food and energy rose 2.6%.
People who trade money now think a rise in December is likely. They put the chance at roughly 73% to 85%. A higher rate makes loans cost more, which can slow price rises.
levels.why: What happens in America can change loan costs in other countries.

levels.headline: America's central bank held interest rates but may raise them in December
levels.body:
Almost every country has a central bank. America's is called the Federal Reserve. It sets the interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. On 28 October it left the rate where it was. It is between 3.75% and 4%. Its boss, Kevin Warsh, did not say what comes next. But he hinted that he would like higher rates.
He may think that because prices keep rising. In the United States they went up 3.7% in the year to September. That is faster than a month before. Petrol was a big reason.
People who work with money now think the Fed will raise the rate in December. They say the chance is about three in four, or higher. A higher rate makes loans cost more.
levels.why: What happens in America can change loan costs in other countries too.

levels.headline: America's money boss left interest rates alone but may raise them soon
levels.body:
Interest is the extra money you pay back when you borrow. A country's central bank sets a main rate for it. America's central bank is called the Federal Reserve. On 28 October it left its rate where it was. Its boss is Kevin Warsh. He hinted that the rate may go up soon.
Why might it go up? Prices are rising too fast. A snack that cost one dollar a year ago now costs about three or four cents more. Petrol has gone up a lot. The Fed uses higher rates to slow price rises down, because people spend less when borrowing costs more.
Many people who trade money think the Fed will raise the rate in December. They think there is a very good chance.
levels.why: It matters because American rates can change prices and loans elsewhere.

levels.headline: America's bank boss may make borrowing cost more
levels.body:
Every country has a big bank that helps look after its money. America's is called the Federal Reserve. It decides how much extra people pay when they borrow money. This extra is called interest. On 28 October, the bank kept the extra the same. Its boss is called Kevin Warsh.
He hinted that the extra might go up soon. This is because prices are going up too fast. A snack that cost one dollar last year costs a bit more now. The bank wants prices to go up more slowly. Making borrowing cost more is one way to do that. When it costs more, people spend less.
Many people who watch money think the bank will do it in December. Nobody knows for sure yet.
levels.why: It could mean loans cost more for grown-ups.

levels.headline: The big bank in America may make borrowing cost more
levels.body:
Imagine you lend your friend a sticker. When your friend gives it back, they add a small extra sticker to say thank you. The extra sticker is like interest. Grown-ups pay interest when they borrow money. America has a big bank that decides how big the extra should be. It is called the Federal Reserve.
This month, it kept the extra the same. But the boss of the bank hinted it might get bigger soon. The reason is that prices in shops are going up too fast. A bigger extra makes people think harder before they borrow and spend. That can stop prices racing upwards.
Many grown-ups who watch money think the extra will get bigger in December. We have to wait and see.
levels.why: It might make loans cost more for grown-ups.

headline: US midterms on Tuesday: Democrats favoured to win the House as the Senate race looks closer

terms.meaning: US elections held halfway through a president's term, to choose members of Congress.
A poll asking voters which party they would back for Congress, without naming candidates.
A betting-style market where traders buy and sell contracts on the outcome of events.

levels.headline: US midterms on Tuesday: Democrats favoured to win the House as the Senate race looks closer
levels.body:
Americans vote in the midterm elections on Tuesday 3 November, and pre-election coverage points to a likely Democratic win in the House of Representatives, with a closer fight for the Senate. levels.headline: Americans will vote for people to make laws

levels.why: It decides who writes the rules for America.

levels.headline: A big vote is coming in America

headline: Burnham urges devolved governments to 'work with me' as first National Economic Council for the nations meets

levels.headline: Burnham urges devolved governments to 'work with me' as first National Economic Council for the nations meets
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called on the devolved governments to work with him on giving every part of the UK more power. In a GOV.UK statement headlined "Work with me to empower every single part of the UK", he set out an offer of partnership on models of regional empowerment.
The message came as Mr Burnham convened the first National Economic Council for the nations, which met in Glasgow on 30 October. The meeting brought the UK Government together with the devolved administrations in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to talk about the economy.
The release also said the Chancellor, John Healey, had given families more breathing space and businesses more investment support in his Budget. It does not set out new laws or spending, so the practical outcome of the council is not yet clear. Devolved governments control areas such as health and education.
levels.why: How power and money are shared between London and the nations affects services across the UK.

levels.headline: Burnham asks devolved governments to 'work with me' at first nations economic meeting

levels.headline: The Prime Minister asks Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to work with him

levels.headline: The Prime Minister asks Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to work with him

levels.why: It is about how the different parts of the country share power.

levels.why: It is about everyone in the country working together.

headline: Tusk urges Polish president to confirm judges as Constitutional Tribunal crisis deepens

terms.meaning: Poland's top court for deciding whether laws and government actions fit the constitution.

levels.headline: Tusk urges Polish president to confirm judges as Constitutional Tribunal crisis deepens
levels.body:
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk called on President Karol Nawrocki on Monday 2 November to confirm judges elected by parliament to the Constitutional Tribunal, saying the conflict can be resolved simply and without changing the constitution, Euronews reported.
The crisis escalated on Friday 30 October, when the Tribunal's president, Bogdan Święczkowski, was suspended. Protesters and riot police faced each other outside the court, and Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska announced she was taking over its leadership. Mr Nawrocki then went to the building overnight, and footage showed scuffles with judges. His side called it a forcible takeover, and the Tribunal called it a judicial "coup d'état".
The roots go back to March, when Mr Nawrocki accepted the oaths of two newly elected judges but refused four others. The European Commission said parliament has the right to appoint judges. The Tribunal's judges hold a General Assembly on Tuesday 3 November at 15:30.
levels.why: The dispute is about who controls Poland's highest court and how far the rule of law is respected.

levels.headline: A fight over Poland's top court is getting worse

Poland has a top court called the Constitutional Tribunal. It decides if laws follow the country's main rulebook, the constitution. Now two leaders disagree about it. levels.why: It is about who controls the court that checks the government.

levels.headline: Poland's leaders are fighting about the country's top court

Poland has a top court called the Constitutional Tribunal. Its job is to check that laws follow the constitution, which is the country's main set of rules. Right now, the Prime Minister, Donald Tusk, and the President, Karol Nawrocki, disagree about who should be a judge there.

Mr Tusk says the President should say yes to the judges. The judges meet on Tuesday.

levels.headline: Two leaders in Poland are arguing about the top court

levels.why: It is about who gets to choose the people who check the law.

levels.headline: Poland's leaders are arguing about who should be a judge

Judges are people who decide if something is fair under the law. Poland has an important group of judges. They are called the Constitutional Tribunal. They make sure that new laws fit the rules of the country.

levels.headline: Two leaders in Poland cannot agree about judges

levels.why: Fair judges help keep a country fair for everyone.

levels.headline: Two grown-ups in Poland are arguing about judges

A judge is a person whose job is to decide what is fair. In Poland, some judges work in a very important group. Two grown-ups cannot agree about who should be in that group. They are like two team captains who cannot agree who should be on the team.

This week, lots of people went outside the building where the judges work. They wanted to show how they feel. Police stood nearby to keep everyone safe. On Tuesday, the judges will have a meeting. Everyone hopes the grown-ups can solve it.
levels.why: Fair judges help everyone get treated fairly.

headline: Cost-of-living protests turn violent in Frankfurt and Paris on a third weekend of youth-led rallies

terms.meaning: The amount of money people need to cover basics such as food, fuel and housing.
A protest tactic in which people dress in black and cover their faces.
French police officers who are part of the military.

levels.headline: Cost-of-living protests turn violent in Frankfurt and Paris on a third weekend of youth-led rallies
levels.body:
Youth-led protests over the rising cost of living spread across Europe again at the weekend. In Frankfurt, downtown saw looting and violence after a demonstration, with rioters smashing shopfronts and stealing goods, including weapons from a gun shop that police later retrieved. Police said Molotov cocktails were thrown at officers.
In Paris, France opened an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at security forces. Police said they had singled out three suspects dressed in Black Bloc style. About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed nationally for the Halloween weekend.
The worst day was 17 October, when the government reported around 1,200 arrests and 150 officers injured. Fuel prices are a key grievance, though economists disagree how far energy costs explain the unrest. The French Senate passed a "Rioters Pay" bill that could make protesters pay up to €10,000, which still needs further approval.
levels.why: The protests show how high prices are straining politics across Europe.

levels.headline: People in Europe are upset because things cost too much
levels.body:

France may make a new rule. People who break things in a riot would have to pay for the damage, up to about ten thousand euros. Most people want protests to be safe.

headline: Russia resumes attacks on Ukraine's Kherson region after local truce ends, Kyiv says

levels.headline: Russia resumes attacks on Ukraine's Kherson region after local truce ends, Kyiv says
levels.body:
Russia has resumed attacks on Ukraine's Kherson region after a local truce ended, Kyiv said on Monday 2 November. Ukraine's human rights ombudsman said the ceasefire, which was in effect from 27 October to 1 November, had ended. A senior Ukrainian figure told AFP that Russia refused a Ukrainian offer to extend it.
A drone strike on a car in Kherson's Korabelny district wounded a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man, according to local authorities. The truce, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, had allowed a humanitarian mission to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, from which residents left.
Both sides reported that their air-raid alert apps were hit by cyberattacks as the truce ended. Ukraine's air force said its app was probably subject to hostile interference, and Moscow's emergencies ministry described a "massive cyberattack". US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are due to resume this month, while the Kremlin has repeatedly rejected calls for a wider ceasefire.
levels.why: The end of the truce shows how hard it is to build a wider peace.
